narrative:
The model determined that you have an 80% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this predicted risk is so high, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence. Placing in the bottom decile (1 out of 10) is far below the average of roughly 6 among accepted students, and this low standing strongly pushed the prediction toward failure. Next in importance was your LSAT score of 24.5, well under the 37-point average of accepted applicants; this gap also pulled the outcome heavily toward not passing. Finally, your first-year ranking in the lowest decile (again 1 versus an average near 6) added further weight in the same negative direction.

Taken together, these academic performance signals told the model you were very likely to struggle with the bar exam. Your family income, undergraduate GPA of 2.2, full-time study plans, gender, and race played no role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Stronger grades and test scores in a future application would substantially lower your predicted risk and open the door to admission.
